quiz.q: Zomato's server needs Domino's pizza types, protected by OAuth. No user data or browser is involved. Which grant type fits?
quiz.explain: Client credentials is for server-to-server communication on common data that no individual owns; the token is generated from client ID + secret alone.

quiz.q: Why can the client credentials flow have fewer steps than the authorization code flow?
options: It doesn't use tokens at all
No browser is involved — it is server-to-server over a secure network
It reuses the user's Facebook session
quiz.explain: With no browser front end nothing is exposed, so the client sends its credentials directly to the token endpoint without an authorization code.

quiz.q: A client's token is valid 10:00–11:00. It sends a request at 11:05 with the same token. What happens?
options: The request succeeds because the token was valid earlier
The token is invalid (expired), so the client must generate a new token
The resource server refreshes the token automatically
quiz.explain: After expiry the token is invalid; the client generates a new one and reuses it until that one expires.

quiz.q: In which HTTP header is the access token sent?
quiz.explain: The token is sent in the Authorization header with each API request.

quiz.q: Your experience API calls an OAuth-protected process API. Where should Mule keep the token for reuse across requests?
quiz.explain: A variable lives only for one request/event; a database works but every read/write is a costly external call. Object Store is temporary storage reusable across requests.

quiz.q: A client caches a token that is valid for 1 hour. How long should it cache it, per the class?
options: Slightly less than the lifetime, e.g. about 55 minutes
Forever, until the server rejects it
quiz.explain: Caching a bit less than the validity (e.g. 55 of 60 minutes) means the cached token expires before the real one, and a new token is then generated.

quiz.q: Zomato's backend sends client credentials plus Ramesh's username/password to its own token endpoint to fetch his order history. Which grant is this?
quiz.explain: The resource owner's password is sent to get the token, to access the user's own data. Its drawback: less secure, since the client handles the user's password.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of a JWT, in order?
quiz.explain: A JWT is header.payload.signature — Base64-encoded and separated by dots.

quiz.q: You paste a JWT into jwt.io and can read the payload. What does that tell you?
options: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode the header and payload
quiz.explain: JWT security comes from the signature (tampering is detected), not from hiding the content, so don't put secrets in the payload.

quiz.q: A client sends 10,000 requests per hour with an OAuth token. What problem does the JWT validation policy remove?
options: Generating a new token for every request
Calling the authorization server to validate the token on every request
Sending the client secret on every request
Caching the token in Object Store
quiz.explain: With plain OAuth validation the API asks the authorization server to validate each request; JWT validation verifies the signature locally at the gateway.

quiz.q: With JWT validation, what is configured in API Manager to verify tokens?
quiz.explain: The authorization server signs the JWT with its private certificate (never shared) and gives the matching public certificate, which the gateway uses to check the signature.

quiz.q: The authorization server rotates its private certificate, but your JWT policy uses a manually configured public certificate that nobody updates. What happens?
options: Only one request fails, then it self-heals
The gateway falls back to calling the authorization server
quiz.explain: With a static certificate, all requests fail until someone updates it. Automatic fetching from a URL means at most one or two requests fail.

cards.back: Client sends client ID + client secret to the token endpoint to get a token. Server-to-server, no user involved — the grant mostly used for APIs.

cards.front: Why client credentials instead of authorization code for APIs?
cards.back: No user or browser is involved and the data isn't owned by an individual user; authorization code is for users granting a third-party app access to their data.
Client sends client credentials + the user's username/password to get a token, to access that user's own data. Drawback: less secure — the client handles the password.
**Authorization code**: third-party sign-in, user-owned data. **Client credentials**: server-to-server, common data. **Password**: user's own data on the client's own system.

cards.front: What do we give a client of our OAuth-protected API?
cards.back: Client ID/secret, the token endpoint details (how to request a token), and our API details.
URL of the authorization server that issues tokens.

cards.front: How should a client handle token expiry?
cards.back: Reuse the token while valid (cache it slightly shorter than its lifetime, e.g. 55 of 60 min); regenerate after expiry.

cards.front: Why not keep a token in a variable?
cards.back: A variable lives only while one request is processed; the next request has no access to it.

cards.front: Where to store an OAuth token in Mule?
cards.back: In an **Object Store** — variables die after each request, and a database adds costly external calls.
Less load on the authorization server, more speed, less resource use.
One login across company apps via an identity provider (e.g. Okta, Auth0) — often also used as the OAuth authorization server.
JSON Web Token: a compact, self-contained token — **header.payload.signature**, Base64-encoded and dot-separated.
No — it is Base64 encoded; anyone can decode it (e.g. on jwt.io). The signature protects integrity.
A reversible encoding format — not encryption (which uses a key/algorithm).
Red = header, purple = payload, blue = signature.

cards.front: JWT validation vs. OAuth token validation
cards.back: OAuth validation calls the authorization server for each request; JWT validation verifies the signature locally at the gateway with the public certificate.

cards.front: Private vs. public certificate in JWT
cards.back: Authorization server signs with the **private** one (never shared); the **public** one is configured in API Manager to verify signatures.

cards.front: Why fetch the public certificate automatically?
cards.back: If the issuer rotates its private key, a manually configured certificate breaks all requests; automatic refresh picks up the new one.
I give you a sample of my signature (public cert) first; if a postman forges the letter, you compare signatures and detect it.
HS256: symmetric — same shared secret signs and verifies. RS256: asymmetric — private key signs, public key verifies.
Token generated using client credentials · no ownership of resources, data is common to everyone · server-to-server communication.
